reading.value: Quick reference A verified corpus bundle Terms for linking corpus bytes to source provenance and understanding the limits of byte verification. Canonical manifest A complete corpus record with one fixed byte representation, including file paths, roles, counts, digests and source provenance. The verifier rejects a different representation rather than silently rewriting it. Corpus bundle The selected raw text sources together with their manifest and provenance files. In this offline fixture, two raw sources share one license file and one attribution file. Dataset artifact identity The SHA-256 digest of the complete canonical manifest. It identifies the corpus record through its provenance and recorded file digests; actual files still need verification. It is not a signature or permission certificate. Raw held-out source The separately acquired text source reserved from the raw training source. Its source filename does not define the final course validation or test split. Retained source prefix The initial bytes of one selected raw source that have been stored and recorded during incomplete acquisition. Recovery rehashes those bytes; resumed delivery must match the same representation validator and final source digest. Source provenance The record connecting selected corpus bytes to their source revision, requested and resolved endpoints, license text and attribution. It does not by itself establish permission or suitability.

This acquisition boundary identifies and verifies corpus inputs before later filtering and tokenization; the offline fixture is not acquired TinyStories or Chapter 42's real input." } --- import RustSource from "../../../components/RustSource.astro"; {/* chapter-section:worked-example */} ## The problem: a downloaded file does not identify a training corpus An LLM learns from the text supplied to its training pipeline. A filename alone does not tell you which text was supplied. Two files named `train.txt` can contain different bytes, and a complete download can still come from the wrong source revision. Even the right text is insufficient for a reproducible corpus record if its source, license text or attribution has been lost. The acquisition boundary needs two kinds of evidence together: a record of the selected sources and their provenance, and checks that the available files match that record. This chapter builds that boundary. It does not clean the text, choose final training splits or establish that the corpus is safe or useful. ## Start with a complete, tiny corpus bundle The example uses course-authored test bytes, not a downloaded training dataset. It has two raw text sources and two shared provenance files: | File in the bundle | Exact bytes represented as a Rust literal | Byte count | | --- | --- | --- | | `raw/train.txt` | `b"abc"` | $3$ | | `raw/valid.txt` | `b"hello\n"` | $6$ | | `provenance/LICENSE.txt` | `b"fixture-only\n"` | $13$ | | `provenance/ATTRIBUTION.txt` | `b"course-authored fixture\n"` | $24$ | In these literals, `\n` represents one newline byte, not a backslash followed by the letter `n`. The two raw sources contain $3+6=9$ bytes. The four payload files in the table contain $3+6+13+24=46$ bytes; this count excludes the manifest record introduced below. Both source records refer to the same license and attribution files, so those shared files are counted once in the inventory. The fixture's license identifier is `LicenseRef-Course-Test-Only`. Its records mark redistribution as `not-approved`. Those values describe this test fixture; they do not grant permission for a real corpus or a model trained from one. Likewise, the name `valid.txt` identifies a raw held-out source here, not the final validation split that a later chapter will construct. {/* chapter-section:formula */} ## The solution: identify the record, then verify every file A **manifest** is the record describing the bundle. Each payload entry names a relative path, a role, a media type, an exact byte count and a SHA-256 digest. Each source record also identifies the selected source revision, requested URL, resolved endpoint, license and attribution. These fields connect a source to its bytes and provenance instead of leaving them as unrelated notes. The manifest receives one fixed byte representation: compact UTF-8 JSON, object keys in byte-sorted order, declared array order and exactly one final newline. That representation is called **canonical**. Its purpose is to prevent harmless formatting choices, such as indentation, from giving the same record multiple identities. An incoming manifest with a different representation is rejected; the verifier does not quietly rewrite it. The bundle identity is $$ \mathrm{artifact\_id}=\operatorname{SHA256}(\mathrm{canonical\_manifest\_bytes}) $$ {/* chapter-section:symbol-glossary */} ## What the identity formula means Here $\mathrm{canonical\_manifest\_bytes}$ means the complete canonical record, including the payload digests and source provenance. $\operatorname{SHA256}$ maps those bytes to a $256$-bit digest. $\mathrm{artifact\_id}$ is that digest, usually displayed as $64$ hexadecimal characters. It identifies the record; it is not a signature or a certificate of legal permission, privacy or language quality. The raw files are represented in the identity through their recorded byte counts and digests. The verifier must still read the actual files and compare them with those entries. Hashing a manifest does not prove that its claimed files exist. The verifier performs three checks in order: 1. Validate the manifest against the selected source policy, including both raw sources and their provenance references. 2. Check the payload inventory. All four listed files must exist as regular, non-linked files; missing or unlisted files cause refusal. 3. Read each file in bounded chunks, count its bytes and calculate its digest. Accept the bundle only when every count and digest matches. {/* chapter-section:rust-implementation */} SHA-256 calculation and JSON parsing use supporting libraries. Rust owns the course-specific source policy, inventory checks, byte comparisons and admission decision. ### Two changes that expose the boundary Replacing `b"abc"` with `b"abd"` preserves the train file's $3$-byte length. A size-only check accepts the replacement. The full verifier rejects it with `Hash`, because the observed digest differs from the selected manifest entry. This is a file-byte check, not evidence about what either text would teach a model. Changing the attribution file to `b"course-authored fixture v2\n"` instead changes that file to $27$ bytes. Rebuilding a consistent manifest updates its attribution entry and both sources' attribution references. The resulting bundle identity differs, although the two raw text digests remain unchanged. The new complete payload totals $49$ bytes. The identity therefore distinguishes provenance changes as well as raw-text changes. Selected fields from the actual offline fixture report are shown below. The manifest occupies $3084$ bytes separately from the $46$ payload bytes. The scope value keeps this result identified as a synthetic fixture, not an acquired training dataset. ```json { "artifact_id": "569de16c16720f73aca07de6a3184b779b80700c3f5f8eefc01f60fea3019b89", "artifact_manifest_bytes": 3084, "inventoried_files": 4, "logical_sources": 2, "raw_bytes": 9, "scope": "synthetic-offline-fixture", "total_payload_bytes": 46 } ``` The example executable runs only this offline fixture and prints its report. It does not download a training corpus. ## Interrupted acquisition must not erase earlier work Acquisition can stop between receiving bytes and completing a source. A resumed request must continue the same selected source and preserve the acquisition's limits; starting a new process must not grant a new byte budget or deadline. In the fixture, the first request retains `b"ab"`, a $2$-byte prefix of the $3$-byte train source. After restart, Rust rehashes that retained prefix and checks its recorded digest. Receiving `b"c"` brings the retained length to $3$ bytes, but completion still requires an explicit end-of-body observation and the final digest check. The held-out source is then checked separately. The report records $9$ acknowledged body bytes and request-attempt counts `[2,1]`: two attempts for the train source, one for the held-out source. A complete train source alone is not a complete pair. Body bytes that were read and discarded still consume the transfer budget. For a separate toy ceiling of $10$ bytes, an error response that delivers $2$ discarded bytes leaves only $8$ bytes available. The two raw sources still require $9$ bytes, so the next request is refused before dispatch: $$ 2+9=11>10. $$ Rust reserves a bounded body-read grant before allowing transport to read. If a process stops with an unsettled grant, recovery charges the whole grant as uncertain delivery, once, rather than assuming that no bytes were read. The counter measures bytes delivered through this body-read interface, not every byte buffered by the operating system or every network packet. Corrupt retained prefixes are refused and preserved in quarantine. Recovery does not reset the attempt count, charged bytes or original deadline.
